rounds.proof_sketch: Input shape [128,1] gives size=128. block_size=256. Original: (128+256-1)/256 = 383/256 = 1. Mutated: (128+256+1)/256 = 385/256 = 1. Both compute num_blocks=1. The mutation only produces different num_blocks when size is a multiple of 256 (e.g., size=256 gives original num_blocks=1, mutated num_blocks=2), but size is fixed at 128.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the ceiling division formula from (size + block_size - 1) / block_size to (size + block_size + 1) / block_size. For this to produce a different result, the interval [size+block_size-1, size+block_size+1] must span a multiple of block_size, which occurs only when size ≡ 0 (mod 256). With the fixed input shape [128,1], size=128 is not a multiple of 256, so both formulas compute to num_blocks=1. The kernel launches identically in both cases, and since threads with idx >= size contribute 0.0f (initialized value), the reduction produces the same result. No value-level change to the fixed-shape inputs can trigger a difference.
rounds.kill_strategy: The mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only be observable with input sizes that are exact multiples of 256 (e.g., 256, 512, 768), but the contract fixes size at 128. No value-level variation within the [128,1] shape can expose this mutation.
rounds.recommendations: When mutation testing kernels with launch-configuration calculations, include test cases with sizes that hit boundary conditions in the block/grid calculations — specifically sizes that are exact multiples of block_size, one less, and one more. For this kernel with block_size=256, test shapes like [256,1], [255,1], [257,1], [512,1] etc. in addition to the primary test shape.
